newsitem.title: HONG KONG: AmCham in Hong Kong confident of China MFN renewal.
newsitem.headline: AmCham in Hong Kong confident of China MFN renewal.

text.p: Top representatives of the American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong (AmCham) said on Monday they were confident the United States will renew China's trade privileges for another year.
"I am optimistic, in fact, confident, that MFN (Most Favoured Nation trade status) will be renewed. One way or another, it will be renewed," chairman Douglas Henck told reporters.
Henck met with more than 130 people on the MFN issue during a visit to Washington last week -- including U.S. congressmen and members of President Bill Clinton's administration.

Henck said his delegation of 17 AmCham officials took note of concerns congressmen had raised about China, particularly that freedoms in Hong Kong might be curbed after Beijing takes back the territory.

Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30. The post-handover administration is determined to introduce new curbs on protests and ban foreign funding of local political groups after July 1.
Other concerns were China's human rights record, the growing size of the U.S. trade deficit with China and Beijing's alleged political funding of the U.S. Democratic Party, Henck said.
Henck said while he was confident Clinton will decide to renew China's MFN status, such concerns could be powerful enough to urge congressmen to pass a resolution of disapproval.
"The president is expected to take the stance that MFN will be renewed," Henck said.
"However, it does make a difference if the House even passes it (a resolution of disapproval) the first time. This is a very bad signal for United States-China relations."
Of the people the AmCham delegation met in Washington, 44 percent were in favour of China's MFN renewal, while 10 percent were strongly opposed, Henck said.
Some 35 percent were undecided, with most of these people citing uncertainties over Hong Kong's freedoms and way of life after the handover, AmCham said.
But Henck said the delegation made clear China's MFN status was crucial for Hong Kong and that the territory itself wanted China's trade status to be renewed.

"Hong Kong could lose as much as US$30 billion in trade and related industry revenues. Gross domestic product growth would likely be curtailed by about three percentage points," Amcham said. "Approximately 86,000 jobs could be lost."
